opus-5.5.text:
I think there are really three layers to it, and people often only look at the first one.

The first layer is fidelity: does the simulation reproduce what you can actually measure in the real world? If you're simulating a robot arm grasping objects, do the contact forces, the friction, the way things slip and deform, match what you see when you run the same motion on real hardware? That's the most intuitive test, and it matters, but it's also the easiest to over-optimize. You can spend years making one scenario look perfect and still have a simulator that's not very useful.

The second layer, and to me the more important one, is transfer. A simulation is ultimately a tool. You build it so that something learned or designed inside it works outside it. So the real question is: if I train a policy or tune a controller in simulation, how much performance do I lose when I deploy it in reality? The sim-to-real gap is the honest metric. Sometimes a simulator that looks less realistic transfers better, because it captures the right variations, the right distribution of uncertainty, rather than one exact picture of the world. Being right about the *range* of what can happen often matters more than being precisely right about one case.

The third layer is cost and scalability. A good simulation has to be fast enough, cheap enough, and easy enough to generate diverse scenarios that you can actually use it at scale. If it takes a week of an engineer's time to build each environment, it doesn't matter how accurate it is. The value of simulation comes from doing millions of trials you could never afford in the physical world.

So when I evaluate a simulation, I ask: does it match reality where it counts, does what I learn in it survive contact with the real world, and can I run it at the scale where it actually changes what's possible? If it only satisfies the first, it's a nice demo. If it satisfies all three, it's infrastructure.

r001.rationale: It identifies transfer as a key criterion and asks whether a policy trained in simulation retains performance when deployed in reality.

r002.rationale: It discusses matching measurable physical behavior and sim-to-real transfer, but does not state that deployability requires sufficiently accurate transfer of real-world physical parameters into the simulation.

r003.rationale: It mentions building environments and generating diverse scenarios, but does not identify high-quality assets and scenes as a prerequisite.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question we argue about a lot internally, because the honest answer is that there's no single number. But let me try to break down how I actually think about it.

The first thing is: a simulation is only good relative to a purpose. If you ask "is this simulation good" without saying what you want to do with it, I can't answer. A simulation that's great for training a robot to grasp objects might be terrible for training it to walk, because the physics that matters is completely different. Contact dynamics, friction, soft materials—those are the hard parts, and you make different compromises depending on what you care about.

So the first test I apply is a transfer test. You train something in simulation, you deploy it in the real world, and you measure how much performance you lose. If the gap is small, the simulation is good for that task. If the gap is large, it isn't, no matter how pretty the rendering looks. People get seduced by visual fidelity, but visual realism and physical realism are almost unrelated. I've seen gorgeous simulators that are useless for control, and ugly ones that transfer beautifully.

The second thing I look at is whether the simulation gets the distribution right, not just individual cases. Real environments are messy and varied. A good simulation should produce the kinds of edge cases you'll encounter in the real world, including ones you didn't think to program in. If your simulator only ever generates the scenarios you already imagined, it's really just a test suite dressed up as a world. That's why randomization matters so much—not because any single randomized sample is realistic, but because the spread covers what reality might throw at you.

Third, and this one is less talked about: speed and controllability. A simulation that's perfectly accurate but runs at real-time speed is almost useless for learning, because the whole point is to compress years of experience into hours. And you need to be able to reset it, perturb it, replay it, and ask counterfactual questions. The real world doesn't let you rewind. The simulation should.

And then there's a subtler criterion. A good simulation should fail in ways that are legible. When the policy does something strange in the real world, you want to be able to trace it back and say, "ah, the simulator assumed rigid bodies here, and this object deforms." If the failure modes are mysterious, you can't iterate.

So if I had to compress it: does it transfer, does it cover the distribution, can you run it fast and poke at it, and do you understand where it's lying to you. Everything else is secondary.

r001.rationale: It calls deployment in the real world a transfer test and says a small performance gap indicates a good simulation for that task.

r002.rationale: It discusses task-dependent physics and physical realism, but does not state that deployment requires accurately transferring real-world physical parameters into the simulation.

r003.rationale: It does not identify high-quality assets or scenes as a prerequisite.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking: good for what? A simulation is always a simplification, so the question is whether it preserves the things that matter for the problem you’re trying to solve.

Then I’d compare it with observations it wasn’t tuned on. Does it reproduce the relevant behavior? Does it still work when you change the conditions? And are the results robust, or do small changes in assumptions produce completely different conclusions?

A simulation can look very convincing and still be wrong. For me, a good one helps you make reliable predictions or decisions—and makes clear where you should stop trusting it.

sol-6.1.text: I’d start by asking what the simulation is meant to help us understand or decide. A simulation can look very realistic and still get the important behavior wrong. So I’d compare its predictions with observations, especially data that weren’t used to build or tune it. Then I’d check how sensitive the results are to its assumptions and inputs. For me, a good simulation captures the behavior that matters for the question, makes its uncertainty clear, and helps us understand where its predictions stop being reliable.
